newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia sends law on opposition wins to parliament.
newsitem.headline: Serbia sends law on opposition wins to parliament.

text.p: Serbia's socialist government moved swiftly to reinstate opposition election victories on Wednesday by approving a draft law and sending it to parliament after months of massive, relentless street protests.

The official Yugoslav news agency Tanjug said the draft law recognising the opposition's municipal wins on November 17 in 14 cities and towns, including Belgrade, had been approved by the government and had been sent to parliament.

Serbia's opposition, students and professional groups have mounted 78 days of rallies after Serbian President Slobodan Milosvic's ruling socialists annulled the results on grounds of unspecified "irregularities".
State radio said parliament would meet in extraordinary session next Tuesday to consider the draft law.
The autocratic Milosevic suddenly announced on Tuesday that he was asking parliament to reinstate the results.

On Sunday he had ordered his anti-riot police to forcibly break up the demonstrations. Repeated baton charges left scores injured in the worst street violence seen in the capital for years, and prompted an international outcry.
On Wednesday afternoon, tens of thousands of demonstrators thronged central Belgrade, keeping up pressure on Milosevic to deliver on his promise.

Iron-grey ranks of paramilitary police were out in strength too. This time they did not leave their automatic rifles behind in their buses as usual but carried them slung over their shoulders, witnesses said.
Teargas guns and CS gas cartridges were also within reach.
Leaders of Serbia's three-party opposition coalition, while giving a cautious welcome to the apparent climbdown, had nevertheless insisted on continuing the protests.

Earlier, before news that the draft law had been prepared and was being sent to parliament, many people in the 50,000-strong throng packing the tree-lined avenues and cobbled pedestrian precincts of central Belgrade expressed doubt.

"I do not trust them at all -- even when I buy (the pro-government newspaper) Politika, I check the date to see if it's correct," opposition politician Vuk Draskovic told the marchers, who whistled, stamped, cheered and blew horns.
"We will sooner have babies before they recognise anything," said economist Zarko Sakic, 40.
"I was beaten six times and if need be would let them beat me 20 times more because this is my way to protest against this lying regime," said a shabbily dressed man in his 30s.

An engineer in suit and tie shrugged. "All of what we do is completely ridiculous but I will miss the demonstrations when they end...people found a lot of wit in them, high spirits, new friends and new loves," he said.
The scepticsm was shared by foreign governments.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette had said he hoped Milosevic's decision was not simply a delaying tactic.
Washington said it welcomed the move "as a first step in the right direction in Serbia".

Quoting the Serbian information ministry, Tanjug said the government accepted that Serbia's relations with the OSCE and international community generally outweighed the importance of any electoral dispute.
The 54-nation OSCE, from which Yugoslavia has been suspended, had verified that Zajedno won the municipal vote in the 14 towns and cities without "irregularities".
But the opposition also demands an independent judiciary and free media ahead of parliamentary and presidential elections due by the end of this year.
Opposition leaders have repeatedly urged their supporters to avoid provoking the police into further clashes.
"Emotions are often quicker than reason -- many people have been beaten -- but please, please, clench your teeth and understand every blow you get is also a medal," said Draskovic.
"Do not give them any motive to beat us -- go home after the protest," he told Wednesday's demonstrators.
Municipal councils have little power, but they do control regional media, including local television stations.
